name: HTML & CSS
author: Recurse
subject: web
description: Semantic, accessible HTML and forms, then CSS: specificity, the box model, flexbox, grid, media queries and variables.

lesson.intro: Every web page is HTML for structure and meaning, plus CSS for presentation. Good HTML makes a page usable by everyone, including keyboard and screen reader users, and good CSS turns it into a layout that works on any screen. This lesson covers semantic markup and accessible forms, then how CSS decides which rule wins, the box model, flexbox, grid, responsive design and CSS variables.
objectives: Structure a page with semantic, accessible HTML: landmarks, headings, alt text and native controls
Build forms with labels, names, the right button types and the right method
Predict which CSS rule wins using the cascade and specificity
Size and space boxes with the box model, box-sizing and relative units
Lay out pages with flexbox and grid, and make them responsive with media queries and CSS variables

sections.title: How an HTML page is put together
sections.body:
Open any website, right-click, choose View Source, and you will find the same skeleton every time. **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure and meaning of content: this is a heading, this is a list, this is a form. **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) describes how it looks. Keeping the two apart is what lets one stylesheet restyle a whole site. HTML is made of **elements**, written as tags: `

` opens a paragraph and `

` closes it. Opening tags can carry **attributes**, like `href` in `` or `lang` in ``. A few elements are **void** and have no closing tag, such as ``, ``, `` and `
`. Elements nest like boxes inside boxes and must close in reverse order: `

Hi

`, never `

Hi

`. Every page has the same outer structure: - `` tells the browser to use modern standards mode. - `` wraps everything and declares the language, which screen readers and translation tools rely on. - `` holds information *about* the page that is not displayed in it: the character encoding, the viewport settings for phones, the `` shown in the browser tab and in search results, and links to stylesheets. - `<body>` holds everything the user actually sees. By default most elements are either **block** or **inline**. Block elements (`<div>`, `<p>`, `<h1>`, `<ul>`, `<section>`) start on a new line and stretch to the full available width. Inline elements (`<span>`, `<a>`, `<strong>`, `<img>`) flow inside a line of text and are only as wide as their content. CSS can change this, but the defaults explain many surprising layouts. Browsers are forgiving and display broken HTML anyway, guessing what you meant. Those guesses differ between browsers and confuse assistive technology, so run your markup through a validator and fix what it reports.

Lamp Shop

Hand-made lamps, shipped in two days.
sections.pitfall: Putting visible content in the head, or the title and meta tags in the body. The head is for information about the page; everything the user should see goes in the body.

check.question: Which of these is a void element, written without a closing tag?
check.explanation: An img has no content of its own, so it has no closing tag; its information lives in attributes like src and alt. Paragraphs, spans and titles wrap content and must be closed.

sections.title: Semantic HTML
sections.body:
Two pages can look identical while one is built from meaningful elements and the other from a pile of `<div>`s. To a sighted mouse user they are the same page. To a screen reader user, a keyboard user or a search engine they are completely different. Choosing elements for what content **is**, not for how it should look, is called **semantic HTML**.

**Landmark** elements outline a page, and screen readers offer shortcuts to jump between them:

- `<header>`: introductory content, such as the logo and site title.
- `<nav>`: a block of major navigation links.
- `<main>`: the page's primary content. Use exactly one.
- `<article>`: a self-contained piece that makes sense on its own, like a blog post or a product card.
- `<section>`: a thematic group of content, usually with its own heading.
- `<aside>`: related content beside the main flow, such as a sidebar.
- `<footer>`: closing information like contact links and copyright.

**Headings** (`<h1>` to `<h6>`) form the document outline, and many screen reader users navigate by them. Use one `<h1>` for the page's main title, then go down one level at a time without skipping. Pick the level by structure; if an `<h2>` looks too big, resize it with CSS.

Use the element that already has the behavior you need. A `<button>` is focusable with Tab, activates with Enter and Space and is announced as a button; a `<div onclick>` does none of that until you rebuild it by hand. Links (`<a href>`) are for **going somewhere**, buttons for **doing something** on the page. Lists belong in `<ul>` or `<ol>`, and tabular data in a `<table>` with header cells.

Every meaningful image needs **alt text** that says what it conveys: `alt="Sales rose 40% from January to March"`, not `alt="chart"`. Purely decorative images get an empty `alt=""`, so screen readers skip them.
sections.code:
Lamp Shop
  • Lamps
  • About

Desk lamps

Brass desk lamp

© 2026 Lamp Shop
sections.pitfall: Building a clickable div and planning to add accessibility later. It is invisible to the keyboard and to screen readers; start with button or a href and style it however you like.

check.question: Which element should wrap a site's main menu of links?
check.explanation: nav marks a block of major navigation links as a landmark, so screen reader users can jump to it or skip it. aside is for related side content, and menu-bar is not an HTML element.

sections.title: Forms and accessibility basics
sections.body:
Forms are where users actually do things on the web: sign up, search, pay. They are also where accessibility problems hurt most, because a form someone cannot complete is a dead end.

A `<form>` sends its fields to the URL in `action`, using the HTTP method in `method`. With `method="get"` the fields go in the query string (`/search?q=lamp`), which suits searches and filters that should be bookmarkable. With `method="post"` they go in the request body, which is right for anything that changes data or includes a password.

Each field needs a few attributes to work properly:

- `name`: the key its value is submitted under. A field without a name is **not submitted at all**.
- `id`: a unique identifier that a `<label for="...">` points at.
- `type`: `email`, `password`, `number`, `date`, `checkbox` and others give the right phone keyboard and built-in validation for free.
- `required`, `minlength`, `pattern` and friends: browser checks before submission. The server must validate again, because anyone can send any request.

A **label** connects text to a field: `<label for="email">Email</label>` with `<input id="email">`. Screen readers read the label as the field's name, and clicking it focuses the field, which gives a bigger tap target. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears as soon as typing starts. Group related radio buttons or checkboxes in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` that names the group.

Buttons inside a form default to `type="submit"`, so any extra button that should not submit needs `type="button"`.

A few habits cover most of accessibility:

- Everything must work with the **keyboard** alone: Tab moves through links, buttons and fields in a sensible order.
- Keep a visible **focus indicator**; never remove the outline without replacing it.
- Text needs enough **color contrast**, and color must never be the only signal: mark an error with text, not just a red border.
- Use **ARIA** attributes only when no native element does the job. The first rule of ARIA is to use the HTML element instead.
sections.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="email">

  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input id="pw" name="password" type="password" minlength="12" required>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Newsletter</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="news" value="weekly"> Weekly</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="news" value="never" checked> Never</label>
  </fieldset>

  <button type="button" onclick="togglePassword()">Show password</button>
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
sections.pitfall: Writing outline: none to hide the focus ring because it looks untidy. Keyboard users then cannot see where they are; restyle it with :focus-visible instead.

check.question: Which method should a login form use, and why?
choices: get, so the login page can be bookmarked
post, so the password goes in the body, not the URL
get, because it is faster than post
Either one, because HTTPS hides the URL anyway
check.explanation: With get, the password would sit in the URL, which ends up in browser history, server logs and analytics, even when the connection is encrypted. post keeps it in the request body.

sections.title: Selectors, the cascade and specificity
sections.body:
You write `.button { background: blue; }` and the button stays gray. Some other rule is winning, and to fix it you need to know how CSS chooses between competing rules.

A CSS **rule** is a selector plus declarations: `.card h2 { color: navy; margin: 0; }`. The common selectors:

- `p` (element), `.card` (class), `#checkout` (id) and `[type="email"]` (attribute).
- `.card h2` (descendant: any h2 inside .card), `.menu > li` (child: direct children only) and `h2 + p` (the p right after an h2).
- Pseudo-classes for states and positions: `a:hover`, `input:focus-visible`, `li:first-child`, `li:nth-child(odd)`, `input:invalid`.
- Pseudo-elements for parts of an element: `p::first-line`, `.price::before`.

When several rules set the same property on the same element, the **cascade** picks the winner in this order:

- **Importance**: `!important` declarations beat normal ones. Avoid them; they start an arms race.
- **Specificity**: the more specific selector wins. Count (ids, classes plus attributes plus pseudo-classes, elements plus pseudo-elements) and compare left to right. `#top a` is (1,0,1) and beats `.menu .link` at (0,2,0), because one id outranks any number of classes. An inline `style="..."` attribute beats every selector.
- **Source order**: when specificity ties, the rule that comes later wins.

Some properties are **inherited**. Text properties such as `color`, `font-family`, `font-size` and `line-height` flow from a parent to its children, which is why setting them on `body` styles the whole page. Box properties such as `border`, `padding`, `margin` and `background` are not inherited.

Good CSS keeps specificity low and flat: style with classes, avoid ids and long descendant chains in selectors, and you will rarely fight the cascade. Browser dev tools list every rule that applies to an element, with the losing declarations crossed out, which makes the cascade easy to debug.
sections.code:
/* HTML:
Home
*/ a { color: black; } /* (0,0,1) */ .link { color: green; } /* (0,1,0) */ nav .link { color: purple; } /* (0,1,1) */ #top a { color: red; } /* (1,0,1) wins: it has an id */ .link { color: orange; } /* (0,1,0) later, but less specific */
sections.pitfall: Fixing a losing rule with !important. It works once and forces the next fix to use it too; raise the specificity a little or reorder the rules instead.

check.question: Two rules both have specificity (0,1,0) and set different colors on the same element. Which color is used?
choices: The color from the rule that appears first
The color from the rule that appears later
A mix of the two colors
Neither; the browser default is used
check.explanation: When importance and specificity tie, source order decides and the later rule wins. That is why the order of stylesheets and rules matters.

sections.title: The box model and units
sections.body:
Every element on a page is a rectangular box, and its size and spacing come from four layers, from the inside out:

- **content**: the text or image itself, sized by `width` and `height`.
- **padding**: space inside the border, which shows the element's background.
- **border**: a line around the padding.
- **margin**: transparent space outside the border that pushes other boxes away.

By default (`box-sizing: content-box`), `width` sets only the content, and padding and border are added on top: `width: 200px` with `padding: 10px` and a 5px border takes 230px. That makes layouts hard to reason about, so almost every modern stylesheet starts by switching every element to `box-sizing: border-box`, where `width` includes padding and border and the box is exactly as wide as you wrote.

Vertical margins between block elements **collapse**: when a 20px bottom margin meets a 30px top margin, the gap is 30px, the larger of the two, not 50px. Horizontal margins never collapse, and margins between flex or grid items do not collapse either.

The `display` property decides how a box takes part in layout. `block` takes a whole line; `inline` flows in text and ignores `width`, `height` and vertical margins; `inline-block` flows in text but respects a size; `none` removes the element from the page; and `flex` and `grid` turn it into a layout container for its children.

CSS has several length units, and choosing well is half of responsive design:

- `px`: a fixed size, fine for borders and small details.
- `rem`: relative to the root (`html`) font size, usually 16px. Ideal for font sizes and spacing, because everything scales when a user raises their browser's default text size.
- `em`: relative to the current element's font size, so it compounds when nested.
- `%`: relative to the parent. `vw` and `vh`: 1% of the viewport's width or height.
sections.pitfall: Setting a width on an inline element such as a span or a link and wondering why nothing changes. Inline boxes ignore width and height; use display: inline-block or block.

check.question: With `box-sizing: border-box`, a box has `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid`. How wide is it on screen?
check.explanation: border-box makes width include padding and border, so the box is exactly 200px and the content area shrinks to 150px. With content-box it would be 200 + 40 + 10 = 250px.

sections.title: Flexbox: layout in one direction
sections.body:
A navigation bar with the logo on the left and links on the right, a row of buttons with even gaps, a sidebar next to the content: these are one-dimensional layouts, a row or a column, and **flexbox** handles them.

Set `display: flex` on a container, and its direct children become **flex items** laid out along the **main axis**. With the default `flex-direction: row`, the main axis runs left to right; with `column`, top to bottom. The **cross axis** is perpendicular to it. Two properties position the items:

- `justify-content` works along the main axis: `flex-start`, `center`, `flex-end`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly`.
- `align-items` works along the cross axis: `stretch` (the default), `center`, `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `baseline`.

Because the axes swap with `flex-direction`, centering horizontally in a column uses `align-items`, not `justify-content`. The famous "center anything" recipe is just both together: `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center`.

A few more properties do most of the remaining work:

- `gap: 1rem` puts space between items, with none at the outer edges.
- `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items move to a new line instead of squeezing or overflowing.
- On an item, `flex: 1` means "grow to take a share of the leftover space". Give a sidebar a fixed width and the content `flex: 1`, and the content fills the rest.
- `margin-left: auto` (or `margin-right: auto` on the item before) absorbs the free space, pushing items to the far end, a neat trick for navigation bars.

Flex properties affect only the container's **direct** children. If something deeper does not move, check which element is actually the flex container.
sections.pitfall: Setting justify-content or align-items on the items, or on an element that is not a flex or grid container. Those properties belong on the container.

check.question: In a flex container with the default `flex-direction: row`, which declaration spreads the items across the row with equal space between them?
check.explanation: In a row the main axis is horizontal, and justify-content distributes items along the main axis. align-items handles the cross axis and has no space-between value.

sections.title: Grid: layout in two dimensions
sections.body:
A photo gallery, a dashboard of cards, a page with header, sidebar, content and footer: these layouts care about rows *and* columns at once. **CSS Grid** is built for exactly that.

`display: grid` on a container plus a column template defines the structure, and the children fill the cells in order:

- `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 1fr` makes three columns: one fixed and two that share the rest. The `fr` unit is a fraction of the remaining free space.
- `repeat(3, 1fr)` is shorthand for `1fr 1fr 1fr`.
- `gap: 1rem` sets the space between rows and columns.
- An item can span several tracks: `grid-column: span 2`, or `grid-column: 1 / -1` to stretch across the full width.

The most useful single line in Grid builds a responsive gallery with no media queries: `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))`. It fits as many columns of at least 200px as the row allows and stretches them to fill it. A phone gets one column; a wide screen gets five.

For page layouts, **named areas** read almost like a drawing. You name regions in `grid-template-areas` and place each child with `grid-area`; rearranging the layout for another screen size means rewriting only the template.

**Flexbox or Grid?** Use flexbox when content flows in one direction and items size themselves: toolbars, button rows, tags. Use grid when the layout should control rows and columns together: page skeletons, galleries, forms with aligned labels. They combine well, with a grid for the page and flexbox inside each card.
sections.pitfall: Writing grid-template-columns: 3fr and expecting three columns. That defines a single column; three equal columns are repeat(3, 1fr).

check.question: What column widths does `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 2fr` give in a 1000px-wide container with no gap?
choices: About 333px for each of the three columns
check.explanation: Fixed tracks are sized first, leaving 800px. That free space is split into 3 fractions of about 267px: one for the 1fr column and two for the 2fr column.

sections.title: Responsive design and CSS variables
sections.body:
Most web traffic now comes from phones, so a page has to work from a 360px phone to a very wide monitor. **Responsive design** means one page whose layout adapts to the space available.

It starts with one line in the head: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`. Without it, mobile browsers pretend the screen is about 980px wide and shrink the page to fit, so the text is tiny and your phone styles never apply.

**Media queries** apply CSS only when a condition holds. The usual strategy is **mobile first**: write the base styles for small screens, then add `min-width` queries that enhance the layout as space grows. `@media (min-width: 768px) { ... }` applies at 768px and wider. Pick breakpoints where *your content* starts to look wrong, not by device models.

Flexible building blocks reduce how many queries you need: `max-width` instead of fixed widths, `rem` units, `img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }` so images never overflow their container, wrapping flex rows and auto-fit grids. Media queries can also respond to user preferences: `prefers-color-scheme: dark` for dark mode and `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` to tone down animation.

**CSS custom properties**, usually called **CSS variables**, keep design values in one place. Their names start with two dashes, and `var()` reads them:

- `:root { --brand: #0b6bcb; --space: 1rem; }` defines them on the root element, so the whole page can use them.
- `color: var(--brand)` uses one, and `var(--brand, navy)` supplies a fallback for when it is not defined.
- Variables **inherit** and follow the cascade, so you can override one in a smaller scope (`.danger { --brand: #c62828; }`) or inside a media query, and every rule that reads it updates.

That last point makes variables perfect for themes: change a handful of them under `prefers-color-scheme: dark` and the whole site switches colors without touching any other rule. And unlike variables in preprocessors such as Sass, CSS variables are live in the browser, so JavaScript can change them at run time.
sections.pitfall: Designing for desktop and then squeezing it down with a pile of max-width overrides. Starting mobile first with min-width queries usually needs less CSS and fewer fights.

check.question: What does `var(--gap, 8px)` give when no element sets --gap?
choices: Nothing, and the whole stylesheet is ignored
check.explanation: The second argument of var() is a fallback used whenever the variable is not defined on the element or inherited from an ancestor.

keyTerms.definition: A piece of HTML made of tags, attributes and content, such as Home.
Choosing elements for what content is (nav, main, button) rather than how it looks.
A region element such as header, nav, main or footer that assistive technology can jump to.
Text tied to a form field with for and id; it names the field and focuses it when clicked.
The part of a CSS rule that chooses which elements it styles.
How CSS picks between conflicting declarations: importance, then specificity, then source order.
A selector's weight, counted as (ids, classes and attributes and pseudo-classes, elements).
Every element as content, padding, border and margin, from the inside out.
Makes width and height include padding and border.
One-dimensional layout along a main axis, controlled by justify-content and align-items.
Two-dimensional layout with rows and columns, using fr units, repeat() and named areas.
A CSS variable such as --brand, read with var() and inherited through the cascade.

summary: HTML says what content is and CSS says how it looks; choose elements by meaning, not appearance.
Landmarks, a clean heading outline, alt text and native buttons and links make a page work with a keyboard and a screen reader.
Form fields need a name to be submitted and a label to be understood, and buttons in a form submit unless they have type="button".
The cascade compares importance, then specificity (ids beat classes beat elements), then source order.
Use box-sizing: border-box and rem units, flexbox for one direction and grid for two.
Go mobile first with the viewport meta tag and min-width queries, and keep design values in CSS variables.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend building their first website why a page made only of divs can look perfect and still be broken, and how they would lay out a header, sidebar, content and footer that also works on a phone.

questions.question: Why is `<button>` better than `<div onclick="save()">` for a Save action?
choices: Divs cannot have click handlers in modern browsers
Buttons load faster and use less memory than divs
It is keyboard-accessible (Tab, Enter, Space) by default
Only buttons can be styled with CSS hover effects
questions.explanation: Buttons come with keyboard focus, key handling and a role that screen readers announce. A div needs tabindex, a role and key handlers added by hand to match, and is easy to get wrong.

questions.question: Which element should wrap the primary content of a page, and appear only once? Type its tag name.
questions.explanation: <main> marks the central content of the page, so screen reader users can jump straight to it past the header and navigation.

questions.question: An accessibility checker flags this markup. What is the problem?
choices: Headings skip from h1 to h4; use h2 and style it with CSS
A paragraph cannot directly follow a heading element
The h1 must be wrapped inside a header element
Headings need an alt attribute for screen readers
questions.explanation: Headings form an outline, and jumping from h1 to h4 suggests missing levels to people navigating by headings. Pick the level by structure and change the look with CSS.

questions.question: Where does the `<title>` element go, and what does it control?
choices: In the body; it is the main visible heading of the page
In the head; it sets the largest heading shown on the page
In the footer; it labels the page when it is printed
In the head; it sets the text shown in the browser tab
questions.explanation: <title> belongs in <head> and is not shown in the page itself; browsers show it in the tab and search engines use it as the result title. The visible main heading is the <h1>.

questions.question: Complete the label so that clicking it focuses the email input.
questions.explanation: A label's for attribute must match the input's id, which is user-email. It is not linked to the name, which is the key used when the form is submitted.

questions.question: A search form uses `method="get"`. Where do the field values end up?
choices: In the URL query string, such as /search?q=lamp
In the request body, hidden from the URL
In a cookie the browser sets for the site
In the page's local storage until submitted
questions.explanation: GET forms put the fields in the query string, which makes results bookmarkable and shareable. That is also why passwords and data-changing forms should use POST.

questions.question: Clicking "Show password" submits the form and reloads the page. Why?
questions.code:
<form action="/login" method="post">
  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input id="pw" name="password" type="password">
  <button onclick="togglePassword()">Show password</button>
  <button type="submit">Log in</button>
</form>
choices: onclick cannot be used on buttons that are inside a form
The form needs method="get" for extra buttons to work
Every button in a form submits it, whatever its type is
Buttons in a form default to type="submit"; add type="button"
questions.explanation: A <button> with no type inside a form is a submit button. After togglePassword() runs, the click submits the form. type="button" makes it do nothing except run its handler.

questions.question: Why should every form field have a `<label>`, even when it already has a placeholder?
questions.answer: A label stays visible while the user types, is announced by screen readers as the field's name, and makes its text clickable to focus the field. A placeholder disappears once typing starts and is not a reliable replacement.
questions.explanation: Placeholders are hints. People who are interrupted mid-form, use screen readers, or have memory difficulties rely on a label that stays put.

questions.question: Write the specificity of `#nav .item a` as three numbers for ids, classes and elements, like 0,2,1.
questions.explanation: #nav is one id, .item is one class, and a is one element, giving (1,1,1).

questions.question: What color is the link?
questions.explanation: #top a is (1,0,1), .menu .link is (0,2,0) and a.link is (0,1,1). The id makes #top a the most specific, so source order never comes into play.

questions.question: A box has `width: 200px; padding: 10px; border: 5px solid;` and the default `box-sizing: content-box`. How many pixels wide is it on screen, including the border?
questions.explanation: With content-box, width covers only the content: 200 + 10 + 10 of padding + 5 + 5 of border = 230. With border-box it would be exactly 200.

questions.question: One paragraph has `margin-bottom: 20px` and the paragraph below it has `margin-top: 30px`. How big is the gap between them?
questions.explanation: Adjacent vertical margins of block elements collapse into one, the size of the larger margin. Horizontal margins never collapse.

questions.question: A flex container has `flex-direction: column`. Which declaration centers its items horizontally?
questions.explanation: In a column the main axis runs vertically, so justify-content centers items vertically. align-items works on the cross axis, which is now horizontal.

questions.question: Complete the rule so the cards form three equal columns.
questions.explanation: repeat(3, 1fr) is shorthand for 1fr 1fr 1fr: three columns sharing the space equally. 3fr alone defines a single column.

questions.question: The links inside .nav should spread out in a row, but justify-content has no effect. Why?
choices: justify-content only works in grid layouts
The container is missing display: flex
space-between also needs a gap value
questions.explanation: justify-content and align-items only apply to flex or grid containers. Without display: flex, .nav is a normal block and its children ignore them.

questions.question: Complete the media query so the sidebar is shown only on screens 900px wide or wider.
questions.explanation: min-width: 900px matches when the viewport is at least 900px wide. max-width would do the opposite, and width: 900px matches only at exactly 900px.

questions.question: A page looks tiny and zoomed out on phones, and its `max-width: 600px` media query never applies there. What is most likely missing?
choices: A max-width on the body element
The lang attribute on the html element
A min-width media query for desktops
The viewport meta tag in the head
questions.explanation: Without <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">, mobile browsers lay the page out about 980px wide and scale it down, so the 600px query never matches.

questions.question: Which of these elements is inline by default, flowing inside a line of text?
questions.explanation: span is the generic inline element: it sits inside text and is only as wide as its content. div, p and section are block elements that start a new line and take the full width.

questions.question: The validator rejects this line. What is wrong?
choices: Links are not allowed inside paragraphs
strong cannot be used inside a link
The tags overlap: strong opens inside a but closes after it
The href value must be a full https:// address
questions.explanation: Elements must close in the reverse order they opened, like nested boxes. Here strong starts inside the link but ends outside it. Write docs now.

questions.question: Match each landmark element to what it should contain.

pairs.right: Introductory content such as the logo and site title
A block of major navigation links
The page's primary content, once per page
Related content beside the main flow, like a sidebar
Closing details such as contact links and copyright

questions.explanation: Landmarks give a page an outline that screen readers can jump through, the same way sighted users scan the layout.

questions.question: Complete the image so a screen reader user gets the same information as a sighted user.
choices: alt="Sales rose 40% from January to March"
alt="Image of a chart about sales"
title="Sales rose 40% from January to March"
questions.explanation: Alt text should convey what the image means in context. "Image of a chart about sales" says a chart exists but not what it shows, a file name is noise, and title is not a substitute for alt: many screen readers and all touch users never get it.

questions.question: Which of these should be a link (`<a href>`) rather than a `<button>`?
choices: Switching dark mode on and off
questions.explanation: Links navigate to another URL; buttons perform an action on the current page. Getting this right matters because links and buttons behave differently for keyboards, screen readers and features like open in new tab.

questions.question: The server receives the POST, but no email value arrives. Why?
choices: The label must come after the input it describes
The input has no name attribute, so it is not submitted
type="email" fields are only sent with method="get"
The button needs an explicit type="submit" to send fields
questions.explanation: Only fields with a name are included in the submission; the name becomes the key, as in email=ada@example.com. The id is only for the label and for scripts and CSS.

questions.question: Which of these help keyboard and screen reader users? Select all that apply.
choices: Visible focus styles on links and buttons
A label for every form field
Using <button> for actions instead of clickable divs
outline: none on :focus for a cleaner look
Placeholder text in place of labels
Marking invalid fields with a red border only
questions.explanation: Focus styles show keyboard users where they are, labels name fields, and buttons bring keyboard support for free. Removing outlines hides focus, placeholders vanish while typing, and color alone fails people who cannot see it.

questions.question: Complete the selector so it styles only the li elements that are direct children of .menu, not items in nested lists.
questions.explanation: > is the child combinator: direct children only. A space matches descendants at any depth, while + and ~ match siblings that come after .menu, not items inside it.

questions.question: Which of these declarations do paragraphs inside the body inherit?
choices: color and font-family, but not border
All three, because everything inherits from body
Only border, because it is declared last
None of them; inheritance needs the inherit keyword
questions.explanation: Text properties like color and font-family inherit, so setting them on body styles the page. Box properties like border do not, or every paragraph would get a red frame.

questions.question: Complete the reset so that width includes padding and border on every element.
questions.explanation: border-box makes the declared width the full width of the box, padding and border included. content-box is the default that adds them on top.

questions.question: How much padding does a paragraph inside .card get?
questions.explanation: rem is relative to the root font size, 16px, so 2rem is 32px no matter where the paragraph sits. em is relative to the element's own font size, here inherited as 20px, so the 2em margin is 40px.

questions.question: Complete the rule so .content fills all the width the sidebar leaves.
questions.explanation: flex: 1 lets the item grow into the free space along the main axis. width: auto on a flex item only fits its content, justify-content belongs on the container, and row is already the default direction.

questions.question: With many tags, they squeeze together and overflow the right edge instead of starting a new line. What is missing?
choices: A larger gap so the tags fit
questions.explanation: Flex items stay on one line by default and shrink, or overflow, to fit. flex-wrap: wrap lets them continue on the next line, and gap keeps the spacing on every line.

questions.question: Complete the rule so the gallery shows as many columns of at least 200px as fit, without any media queries.
questions.explanation: auto-fit creates as many tracks as fit, and minmax(200px, 1fr) makes each one at least 200px and lets them share the leftover space. The column count then changes on its own as the container grows or shrinks.

questions.question: You are building a page skeleton: a header across the top, a sidebar and a main area side by side, and a footer across the bottom. Which tool fits best?
choices: Flexbox, since it handles any layout direction
CSS Grid, because the layout has both rows and columns
Floats, which were designed for page layouts
questions.explanation: The skeleton is two-dimensional: regions line up in rows and columns at once, which grid-template-areas expresses directly. Flexbox is better inside each region, where items flow in one direction.

questions.question: Complete the declaration so the button uses the brand color variable.
questions.explanation: Custom properties are read with var() and keep their two leading dashes. $brand is Sass syntax, and the bare name without var() is not a valid color.

questions.question: The New badge is teal, but the Sale badge is not. Why?
choices: Custom properties only work on div elements
--accent is defined on .card, so only elements inside it inherit it
The .badge rule must come before the .card rule
questions.explanation: Custom properties inherit like color does, so a variable set on .card exists only for .card and its descendants. Define it on :root for global use, or write var(--accent, teal) to give the outside badge a fallback.
